Automated Model Briefing

⚠ AI-generated text — may be wrong, incomplete, or overconfident. This is automated commentary on experimental model output, not flight advice and not a weather forecast. It has not been reviewed by a meteorologist.

Overall Assessment — A solid late-September soaring day with strong thermals and good altitudes, but heavily cloud-dominated at northern sites. A southwest synoptic flow strengthens through the afternoon, making ridge sites workable but requiring careful timing for thermal/ridge transitions.

Site Breakdown

  • Kingsbury Grade: Marginal — wind shifts SW and strengthens to 19 mph by late afternoon, outside the preferred SE ridge window. Best thermal window 10am–2pm with peak w* 452 ft/min and ceiling ~5,200 ft AGL. Sharp thermal caution (lapse rate 9.6 °C/km).
  • Hallelujah: Marginal — heavy cloud cover (95%) and a significant SW wind shift to 19 mph at 14:00. Usable window roughly 10am–2pm with peak w* 457 ft/min and ceiling ~5,700 ft AGL. Sharp thermal caution (lapse rate 10.0 °C/km).
  • Slide Mountain: Marginal — winds quickly ramp to 21–28 mph from the SW through the afternoon. A narrow morning thermal window 9am–12pm exists with peak w* 394 ft/min and ceiling ~2,800 ft AGL. Wind becomes too strong for safe sled runs after 13:00.
  • McClellan: Favorable — best thermal site of the day. Moderate SW winds (14–15 mph) align well with launch after 14:00. Prime thermal window 11:30am–4pm with peak w* 593 ft/min and ceiling 6,400 ft AGL. Sharp thermal caution (lapse rate 10.2 °C/km). Advanced pilots only.
  • West McClellan: Marginal — strong SW winds 18–20 mph after 14:00 within the preferred launch range, but peaked earlier. Workable thermal window 1pm–3pm with peak w* 550 ft/min and ceiling ~6,400 ft AGL. Sharp thermal caution (lapse rate 9.8 °C/km).
  • Peavine Mountain: Unfavorable — 100% cloud cover and wind rapidly escalates to 29–32 mph SW by late afternoon. A brief thermal window 10am–1pm exists but is overshadowed by building wind and overcast conditions.
  • Rainbow Ridge: Unfavorable — 100% cloud cover and hazardous shear (speed shear 9 mph/layer, directional change 37°). Wind direction swings from NE early to SW 15 mph, crossing the preferred E/NE ridge window. Not a safe day for this site.
  • Duck Hill: Favorable for afternoon ridge soaring — SW winds build to 14–19 mph from 14:00–18:00, ideal for the W/NW facing ridge. Thermal window 12:30–3pm with peak w* 565 ft/min and ceiling ~7,600 ft AGL. Also check the 18:00–20:00 evening drainage window with 16–20 mph SW flow. Sharp thermal caution (lapse rate 10.1 °C/km).
  • Daydreams: Favorable — classic SW ridge soaring day with winds 14–20 mph within the preferred 225° ± 30° sector all afternoon. Thermal lift is modest (peak w* 181 ft/min) but consistent from early morning (08:00) through 21:00, making it an all-day ridge/thermal hybrid with a ceiling ~3,900 ft AGL.

Hazards

  • Low-level shear: Speed shear hazardous at Hallelujah (8 mph/layer), Rainbow Ridge (9 mph/layer), Slide Mountain (5 mph/layer), West McClellan (5 mph/layer), Duck Hill (6 mph/layer), and McClellan (6 mph/layer). Exercise caution below 500–3,000 ft AGL where layer jumps exceed 5 mph.
  • Directional shear: Hazardous at Rainbow Ridge (37° layer change). Rotor risk is elevated here and generally downwind of Peavine and Carson Range ridgelines in strong SW flow.
  • Sharp/rough thermals: Lapse rates are dangerously steep (9.6–10.2 °C/km) at Kingsbury, Hallelujah, McClellan, West McClellan, Rainbow Ridge, and Duck Hill. Suitable only for advanced/expert pilots comfortable with aggressive, high-G thermal cores. Thermal turbulence is approaching rough thresholds (σw 1.9–2.0 m/s) at McClellan and West McClellan.
  • Cloud overdevelopment risk: Not indicated by overdevelopment metric, but 95–100% average cloud cover at Hallelujah, Peavine, and Rainbow Ridge suggests extensive cloud streets or cu-filled skies that could limit sun exposure and reduce thermal quality unexpectedly.

Site Forecast ?Top of Thermals (PBLH) — height of the turbulent mixing layer; thermals typically reach this ceiling.

w* — convective velocity scale; higher = stronger thermals (ft/min).
